Three Rivers customs house, new heating apparatus, $1,600.
This is to reconstruct the heating apparatus.

The chief architect tells me that it was put in more than twenty years ago.

Is this a new building ?

Yes, this is in the county of Chambly. The population of the town is 2,757, and the postal revenue $612.92.
* Mr. BENNETT. What is the cost of the building and site ?
The building will cost $10,000. The cost of the site will be small.
Will this building serve any other purpose besides that of the post office '!
It will serve election purposes.
This is for a post office only. In customs, this town is an outport of Montreal. .

This is even worse than the other case we have had under discussion. The appearance of this in the estimates is due to the fact that this town is in the district to be presided over by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Hon. Mr. Prefon-taine) in election time, and he is going to be true to his record in the past to make elections not with prayers alone, but with something else. I have looked up the report of the Post Office Department, and I find that the public are being served there in a building for which a rental of $40 a year is being paid. There is no complaint that the building is not sufficient; nor does it appear that the postmaster makes any complaint that $40 a year is not a sufficiently high rent. And the total revenue of this post office is $612. I am surprised that the Minister of Customs (Hon. Mr. Paterson) sits there with no word of protest against what he would have called in the old days a scandalous and outrageous expenditure. I remember one occasion, under tlie previous government, when the hon. gentleman who, is now Minister of Customs and others of tlie opposition of that day held the House for a whole night to discuss a proposition that was much more defensible than this one.
I know by the way in which you are looking at me, Mr. Chairman (Mr. Macdonald) you would like to have an opportunity to protest against this expenditure. It is refreshing to see these gentlemen, so blatant in the past in their professions of economy, proposing an expenditure of $10,000 for a public building in a town like this. Not only must that building be paid for, but it must be heated and lighted and a. caretaker for it must be paid. I congratulate the Minister of Marine and Fisheries on securing this grant, and I sympathize with the Minister of Public Works, because I know that it is against his will that this grant is going through.

Not only is this a violation of the professions of hon. gentlemen in times past, but it is also an injustice

to many of the larger towns in the province of Ontario. There has been added to my constituency another township and town, a very important town-Meaford. The population is about 2,000 and the revenue from the post office is between $3,000 and $4,000. Money orders to the amount of $25,000 are issued there yearly. That town is left without a post office. There ought to be some principle or rule to guide the government [DOT] in making these grants for public buildings. It is to be regretted that such grants as these are proposed. They involve a flagrant violation of the promises made by hon. gentlemen opposite when in opposition. They may think it very clever; they may think they can ' fix ' a constituency by this means. But it is no credit to the Liberal party. It is something that they will have to defend, and that will always furnish ground of attack on the part of their opponents. It is a shame that a government that came in under such splendid auspices should descend to such a despicable means to keep themselves in office.

The town of Bracebridge which has 3,000 or 4,000 inhabitants was promised a post office building. I see the promises made to that town are being carried out in part by giving them a dock. But they were promised a post office during the last election. I regret that the hon. member for North Ontario (Mr. Grant) is silent, and that the Postmaster General (Hon. Sir William Mulock) is not here to insist on the Minister of Public Works putting in an item for that building. I trust we shall yet hear from the hon. member for North Ontario.

Is it not possible to get a little more light on this subject ? We are putting these estimates through with very inadequate information. What is to be the total cost of this building ? Has the site been secured ? Are the plans prepared ? We seem to be going it blind in most of these cases.
My hon. friend (Mr. Clarke) must admit that I have given that information already.
I did not so understand it. What is to be the total cost ?
I gave that, but I will repeat it. It will cost $10,000.
Ten thousand dollars. In a place with postal receipts of only six hundred dollars ?
Its being the only building in the county is the only defence I can put in, aside from the population and the receipts.

Perhaps the minister will give us the policy of his department on this question. It is rather difficult for us to Mr. THOMSON (Grey).
understand why very much larger towns in other parts of Canada, having a much larger revenue, are overlooked. Now, the minister feels it his duty to grant this request made to him, and we are not complaining of that; but we think the public should understand what is the policy that guides the minister in the erection of public buildings, whether it is the population, whether it is the revenue that is paid into the Customs and Post Office Departments, or whether it is merely a political reason. It is very important that the public should know what policy is guiding him, so that they may know when to come to the government for a public building.

I have explained to the committee the policy with regard to the erection of these buildings. I am willing to admit that the revenue and the population should be the principal considerations. My hon. friend knows that it has 'been the policy to give at least one public building in each county.

I may say that the receipts of the post office at Longueuil, my native town, have been a disgrace to the place for years. To my knowledge petition after petition were sent to the Conservative government during many years, asking for a public building there. But no attention was paid to them, for the reason, I believe, that the town was Liberal. I cannot see any other reason. Since the advent of the present government, in 1896, petitions have been presented time and again, and the people have been promised a new post office. The fact that the town is situated on the south shore of the St. Lawrence, opposite the city of Montreal, probably accounts for the revenue being so small, because the people who go over to Montreal in the daytime take their letters with them and deposit them there. The letters would reach their destination sboner if deposited in Montreal than if deposited in Longueuil. Also many people receive their letters in Montreal instead of Longueuil. The grievance complained of by the people with respect to their post office ought to be remedied and is going to be remedied by the present government. For myself, I have had nothing to do with it. I no longer represent Chambly since 1896, when that county was joined to VerchSres.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: That is what I have just explained.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
It is plain from what has been said by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries that this is more of a job than

ever. He says that a good many people living in Longueuil have their business connections in the city of Montreal as a matter of course, and as a consequence there is little or no necessity for a post office building in that town. He also says that for the last seven years-I suppose he is now taking a fling at the Postmaster General in his absence-in saying the post office in Longueuil has been a disgrace to that town.
I did not say for the last six or seven years. I said that for years gone by, for the last twenty-five or thirty years.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: That only makes it worse. The hon. gentleman says that for many years the people have been complaining of this grievance. There was a course open to them, simply to make a complaint to the Postmaster General that the premises were not sufficient for the post office business, and then it would have been the duty of the Postmaster General either to provide suitable premises or to resign. It was not to be expected that the Minister of Marine and Fisheries would be looking after matters so trivial as the public good of Longueuil, seeing that the more important interests of Montreal took up his attention. Being a suburb of the city of Montreal, the people cross over to Montreal to do their business, and consequently we have only the trifling receipts of $600 at the post office. Yet now the country is to be plunged into an expenditure that will probably run up to $15,000. Moreover, you will require a caretaker for that bulding, you will have to pay the interest on the money, and pay for the heating, lighting and so forth. Once more I congratulate the Minister of Marine and Fisheries that, if he is not given more patronage in his department, he is at least allowed the privilege of dispensing the loaves and fishes to the electors in the district of Montreal.

I wish to draw the attention of the Minister of Public Works to a very important town in East Northumberland, the town of Campbellford. The post office receipts at that office are $3,241 ; money orders, $20,870 ; and the allowance for rent is $140. I am safe in saying that is one of the most flourishing manufacturing towns in that section of the country. I know it has been said that Cobourg has a public building, but I want to draw the attention of the minister to the fact that Cobourg is the county town of the united counties of Northumberland and Durham. Campbellford is between thirty and forty miles from Cobourg, and I think it has strong claims upon the department for additional public buildings. I think there has been a vote this session for Bowmanville, in the county of Durham. I want to draw the hon. minister's attention to the fact that
as there are three or four manufacturing industries at Campbellford, there must be quite a large revenue from the customs and post office. I am satisfied that if the hon. minister will agree to put an amount in the estimates for a building there the town will gladly furnish a site.

I notice that when the hon. minister was in opposition he had a principle in respect to the expenditure of money for public buildings, and perhaps, although the hon. gentleman has been in office for some years, it might be well to refresh his memory in regard to it. In discussing the vote for a post office in 1895, the hon. minister said :
The hon. minister disregards altogether the amount of revenue received under the various departments but that should be recognized as a principle governing the erection of these public buildings irrespective of party reasons.
May I ask the hon. gentleman if lie holds the same opinion now ?
Yes, I hold the same opinion still, and I am trying to carry it out as far as I am personally concerned.

The hon. minister lias not changed his policy in so far as his statement goes, but the practice does not quite live up to the statement. If that be the policy of the hon. gentleman now, would he be good enough to tell us why he has not considered it his duty to recommend an appropriation to erect a public building in Owen Sound, which has been referred to by my hon. friend from North Grey (Mr. Thomson), and which has a population of 10,000 and a revenue of $15,000, while he has conceived it to be his duty to recommend an appropriation for a place which has a revenue of $600 and a population of 2,400 ? The hon. minister has made the statement that it is the policy of the government that one of the principal points, the shire town in each county shall be recognized. May I remind the hon. gentleman that Owen Sound is the county town of Grey. This matter was brought to the hou. gentleman's attention at the last session Of parliament, and he is very well informed as to the condition of things there. Would he be good enough to tell us why it is that in making these further appropriations, Owen Sound has been overlooked ?

I have already told the hou. gentleman that it has not been overlooked. The matter is under consideration, and I did say that the policy which has been laid down by a majority of the members of this House, and which I think is a good policy, that the revenue should be tlie most important factor in connection with these public buildings, ought to be considered. It seems also to be the idea of the majority of the members of the House that one public building should be given to a county. My hon. friend has

said that Owen Sound is entitled to consideration from both of these standpoints, and I acknowledge it.

How am I going to explain to my constituents the principle upon which money of this kind is allocated? Here are two little towns In lower Canada, Longueuil and Acton Vale, one with a population of 1,200, and the other, with receipts altogether from customs, excise and post office of less than $600. The government probably get about $100 a year of revenue from Longueuil. Yet they are building a post office which will involve an expenditure of anywhere from $10,000 to $15,000. The town of Perth has no public building of any kind erected by the government. The receipts from the j)ost office are nearly $6,000 a year, the amount deposited in the post office savings bank is larger than that deposited in any town of a like population in Canada ; the population is a little over 4,000; it has inland revenue receipts of $05,000, and customs receipts of about $30,000. The government are receiving in all about $126,000 a year from the town of Perth, and there is no sum at all given for a public building. If this happened to be located somewhere near Terrebonne or in some of the maritime provinces there would have been a large allowance for a public building. If the proportion of population and revenue considered sufficient to justify the erection of a public building in Nova Scotia or New Brunswick were applied to the town of Perth, nearly every third building would be a public building, but, there is no public building at all.
There are not many more counties to be supplied and the town of Perth will have to be considered.

I would like to ask the hon. minister if he proposes to bring down further supplementary estimates this session ? I can scarcely realize that in face of all that has been said, they will not include so important a town as Owen Sound.
I felt very confident that the government would make some provision this session for a public building there, and I am very much disappointed that it has not been included in these supplementary estimates.
I would therefore ask the hon. minister if he is going to bring down further supplementary estimates this session ?
I cannot answer that question at the present moment.
The hon. minister did not give me any consolation about Campbell-ford.
My hon. friend (Mr. Cochrane) certainly made out a very good case. I have noted the matter, and it will receive consideration.

The constituency of my hon. friend (Mr. Cochrane) is in Ontario. I notice that at Campbeliton, where they have a revenue of $3,800, just the same as Campbellford, and a population of about 1,000, they are spending about $35,000.
Where do you get the population from-the census ?
It is not an Incorporated town as far as is shown by the census, but it is an unincorporated village. Yet, the government purpose spending $35,000 for a public building.
That is in New Brunswick.

It is very similar in name to the town that my hon. friend (Mr. Cochrane) brings to the attention of the hon. minister, but the fact of my hon. friend being in Ontario seems to debar him from getting any assistance towards the erection of a public buillding in Campbellford.

My hon. friend from South Lanark (Hon. Mr. Haggart) has referred to the maritime provinces. I would like to inform him that the maritime provinces are not in this class at all. I have been looking at the post office revenue in Nova Scotia, and I find that there are thirty or forty places without public buildings in that province which have a larger revenue than these two places which are now to have public buildings.
Montreal-barracks for permanent corps, $20,000.
Would the hon. minister please give a full explanation of this item ?

This is a new vote of $20,000 for the erection of a barracks for one unit of the permanent corps at Montreal. The estimated cost is $126,000. We own the site, and the city of Montreal, as I am informed, have placed to our credit $25,000 to be devoted to this object.
Where are those barracks to be ?
On Lafontaine park, formerly known as Logan's Farm.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: What corps is to be brought there ; is it to be a new addition to the strength of the force ?

The idea is to have a battery of garrison artillery and a detachment of infantry-in all, 200 men. It is estimated that the accommodation for these will cost from $100,000 to $125,000, of which the city of Montreal has voted $25,000. It would seem to me very desirable, in the public interest, that in a great city like Montreal there should be at least a small detachment

of the permanent force. It has been found to be very useful in Toronto.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: Does the minister purpose retaining the corps at St. John's ?
It is proposed to transfer the infantry from St. John's to Montreal and to establish a cavalry corps at St. John's.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: There will be an addition to the permanent militia force ?
There is an addition of 200 involved in this.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: The building is to cost $125,000 and $25,000 of that is provided by the municipality of Montreal.
That is it, and the site is now owned by the government.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext:
I heartily endorse the idea of having an institution in Montreal, in which officers, or non-commissioned officers or cadets, could get a military training. As the minister knows, I do not believe that the proper plan for giving that system of instruction is to have a permanent corps, in the ordinary sense of the word. I think it can be accomplished much more economically and much more efficiently by the means which I have already explained to the House.
Quebec drill hall-addition to building, $20,000.
This is to provide for additional ground adjacent to the drill hall
You cannot get any more ground than you have there.

I think that is an error. There may be a small corner in front of the drill! hall that ought to be acquired, but I do not know that it is necessary. The explanation is this. A certain sum of money was contributed by the Quebec government and by the city of Quebec towards the construction of the drill ball originally, and it was understood that the city should have the right to use the building for exhibition purposes, &c. This dual ownership has not worked satisfactorily, and as the military corps have increased in Quebec, it has been found impossible to give them the accommodation they ought to have. The local government and the city have intimated to us that if the government will give the increased accommodation, which is very desirable, they would absolutely give up their title to the drill hall. There are now in the city of Quebec no less than eight different military units.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: Not counting the permanent corps ?
Not counting the permanent corps.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: What is the total strength?

I cannot remember. There is a battery of field artillery; two squadrons of cavalry, the Queen's Own; a regiment of garrison artillery; the 8th and 9th battalions of infantry, both first-rate regiments; No. 1 company, A.S.C.; No. 5 bearer company, and No. 3 field hospital corps. It is absolutely necessary that additional accommodation should be provided, and it seems to me that the offer made by the provincial government and the city of Quebec ought to be accepted.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: It is stated in an evening paper that No. 3 battery is to be removed from Kingston to Ottawa.
That statement is without the slightest foundation; there is not a word of truth in it.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: Is $20,000 the total sum required for this purpose ?
Ves.
I would not like to say that it will be sufficient.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: That is the explanation given to me.
Of course, the Minister of Public Works would know, but I should think that it would cost more.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: What is the status of the government of Canada in relation to the Plains of Abraham ? That ground is being rapidly handed over for' building purposes, and this historic spot, in which the people of Canada have some interest, is being hedged around with houses, so that you can hardly see Wolfe's monument at the present time. It is needless to remark that both the English and the French people regard the Plains of Abraham with some veneration.

The Plains of Abraham were purchased by the Dominion government and handed over to the city of Quebec for a park, to be used only for the purpose of a park, and subject to the right of the Department of Militia and Defence to use the grounds for military purposes.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: There is no building going on upon the plains under these conditions ?
I do not think there is.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext:
The city of Halifax has certain rights in the northern com-

mon of Halifax which are subject to certain conditions imposed by the imperial government, namely, that no buildings shall be put up within a certain distance ; and tin's condition is rigidly adhered to, so that when a little temporary shed was erected on the common a few years ago the imperial government got an injunction to prevent it being continued, although it was of the most flimsy character and was intended to be kept there only a few weeks. If the government have similar rights with, respect to the Plains of Abraham, I think these rights should be enforced, and no buildings should he allowed to be erected there.
The MINISTER OF MILITIA ANI) DEFENCE. I will make inquiries at once. I think our position with respect to the Plains of Abraham is as strong as the position of the imperial government with respect to the Halifax common.
Sherbrooke drill hall. $10,000.

This is one of a number of votes which I am asking the House to authorize for the purpose of furnishing proper quarters for the militia force throughout the Dominion. I feel that we might almost as well give up our organization unless we provide better accommodation, both for tile men and for the arms and accoutrements. The present lack of accommodation has been discouraging to officers and men who give of their time and means for the maintenance of a militia force in Canada. We have had a good deal of complaint in the House from time to time as to the expensiveness of our system, and I think the provision of better quarters for the care of arms and accoutrements will be a measure of economy. We have given the subject a good deal of att?n-tion, and, as the result of conferences witii the officials of the Militia Department, we have come to the conclusion that we can erect a building which will be permanent, substantial and suitable in each of the larger places throughout the Dominion for about $25,000.
I might point out that Sherbrooke is the largest centre in the eastern townships.
I am not speaking specially of Sherbrooke I am speaking generally. My hon. friend will agree with me that we cannot spend from $125,000 to $150,000 in each of these places.
What is the St. Hyacinthe drill hall to cost ?
And you propose to spend the same amount in a place like Sherbrooke ?

I think that in places like Sherbrooke, Belie-Mr. BORDEN (Halifax).
ville and Stratford we can erect a building which will give satisfaction at a cost of about $25,000. It will be an encouragement to the officers and men of the militia force to have this accommodation, and it will protect our property. We all know that many of our valuable guns have been destroyed and the accoutrements have been injured for[DOT] want of proper care, sometimes before they cotdd be used in a second camp.

Sherbrooke is the centre of what the minister is very properly turning into a cavalry district ; so that there will be infantry, cavalry and artillery there, and the town occupies a very important strategic position. 1 think the minister should make provision for a dr'll hall suitable for the wants of the whole district. If he can afford to vote $24,000 for a small centre like St. Hyacinthe, where there are only four companies, surely be ought to be prepared to appropriate $125,000 for a large centre like Sherbrooke, which is surrounded by cavalry, infantry, and artillery.

Not artillery. I may say that it is intended to carry out at St. Hyacinthe the very scheme of organizing cavalry 1o which the hon. gentleman refers. I beiieve it will be an admirable district for recruiting at least one cavalry regiment. In Sherbrooke there is at present one cavalry regiment and one infantry regiment.
Three Rivers custom house-retaining wall, $2,500.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext:
This is to pay the balance of the contract. The work is completed.
St. Louis de Mile End-public building, $10,000.
This is to make provision for the erection of a public building for post office purposes. The population is 10,933.
It seems extraordinary that the post office receipts at that point are only $640.
The receipts go into the Montreal office. The policy of the department seems to be to accommodate the people with these postal stations.
What will the total cost of the building be ?
About $15,000, including the site.

This town will be annexed to the city of Montreal in a short time. Its population is increasing at the rate of about 1.000 a year. It is where the Canadian Pacific Railway locomotive works are situated.
Montreal new postal station-fittings and furniture, $5,000.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: In this particular case we rented a building on very favourable terms on St. Cathar'nes street, and we are establishing a postal station there. This vote is for the fittings and furniture.
What is a postal station as distinguished from a post office ?

As I understand it the idea is that instead of having all the mail sent to the head office, as at present, involving delay in sorting, the mails will be sorted on the train or at the railway station, and sent to the postal stations for distribution, each station serving a certain district of the city.
Magog-public building, $5,000.
Is there any other public building in the same constituency ?

This vote is to make provision for the purchase of a site for the erection of a public building in the town of Magog for post office and customs purposes. The population at the last census was 3,515, the postal revenue $2,500, and the customs revenue, $6,312.
What are the site and the buildings to cost respectively ?
This building will cost about $12,000.
And how much for the site ?

I suppose the site will cost between $500 and $1,000.
Mi*. HUGHES (Victoria). Is there any other public building in the county ?
I understand there is one at Coaticook.
1 think there is a public building at Coaticook, although I am not quite sure. The two towns are at the extreme ends of the county.
Which is the shire town ?
There is no shire town. A circuit court is held for each place, but municipal meetings are held at Ayer's Flat, which is mid-way between the two places, and has a population of 100 or 200.
How does the minister explain his rule that he will only give one public building in each riding '! He seems to be departing from it in this ease.
There are exceptions, and as the Minister of Agriculture has pointed out, there seems to be a town in each end of this riding.

In order to justify these votes, I think that more than one reason is necessary.
Public buildings-Ontario, Belleville armoury, $10,000.

The armoury at Belleville was condemned and ordered to be pulled down. This vote is in accordance with the policy of the department of establishing these headquarters for tlie militia throughout the province.

I do not see any item here for a drill hall for Lindsay. While I had command of the regiment there,
I felt more or less delicacy about asking for the drill shed. I may call attention to the fact that the town has furnished many good military men, and is nearly three times as large as some of the towns in other provinces to which $10,000 and $25,000 halls are being given. I trust the Minister of Militia and the Minister of Public Works will not allow many more estimates to pass through without placing in them an item for a drill shed in Lindsay.
The	MINISTER	OF	MILITIA	AND
DEFENCE. Did I understand my hon. friend to say that Lindsay was considerably larger than towns to which military appropriations are given ?

It is about three times the size of St. Ilyacinthe.
The	MINISTER	OF	MILITIA	ANDDEFENCE. I think	St. Hyacinthe is	much
larger than Lindsay.
The	MINISTER	OF	AGRICULTURE.
It is nearly 15,000.
I hope the kon. minister will be good enough to take this into his serious consideration and let us have a drill shed.
What will this building cost ?

This building is expected to cost about $25,000. I wish it to be distinctly understood that this is one of those buildings that will come under the category of which I have spoken. My chief architect tells me that probably we are making too low an estimate, but I think the architects ought to be able to make arrangements for good headquarters for about that money, and I think that my hon. friend will admit that the Militia Department in making these recommendations and carrying them out has had regard to the necessities of the militia, and has made the recommendations without regard to political considerations. The recommendations made are generally for places where the necessities are urgent, and these are the larger places.
Belleville is headquarters for two infantry regiments and will require a good armoury.
In these places some distinction has to be made. More or less room is required in the armoury according as they are to be used for infantry, or for cavalry and artillery.
Will tenders be publicly called for ?
All these, Mir. Chairman, will be built by contract after tenders are publicly called for.
We ought to be able to see the plans.

The plans ar.e under consideration between the Militia and Public Works Departments.
Peterborough-armoury, $10,000.

The present building in Peterborough is quite unsuited for the requirements of the militia there and the minister is perfectly right in building this drill shed. There are two corps there, in fact, there are parts of three -corps, an infantry regiment, one section of artillery, and a couple of squadrons of cavalry.
What will the building cost ?

About the same as the others-$25,000.
Guelph-armoury, $10,000.
Will this building be of the same size and cost as the others V

At Guelph there are two batteries and one of the largest rifle regiments in the district. In that case there will be additions necessary for the artillery. Except for this, the building for the armoury will be about the same.
What about the site ?
There will be no difficulty about the site.

I may say that this building is very badly needed, as the militia in Guelph are mot at all well provided for. There are ten -companies there. The present building used for the storage of guns is so completely filled that it is difficult to pass through it. There are twelve guns, with limbers, wagons, harness and accoutrements. It is proposed also to have in Guelph a branch of the Army Service Corps, and it will take a building of considerable size to store their equipment. The rifles are now stored in the cellar of the drill shed. It is headquarters also for the regimental band.
Does not the hon. gentleman (Mr. Guthrie) think that he has neglected his constituency when he has allowed this state of things to continue ?

If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Thomson, Grey) Mr. HUGHES (Victoria).
were Minister of Public Works or Minister of Militia, he would acquit the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) of being at all neglectful. He has been very persistent in this demands.

There are two batteries in Guelph, and excellent batteries they are. No doubt the Minister of Militia and the Minister of Public Works will allow for the fact that it will require a larger building than an ordinary drill shed to accommodate the guns ?
I explained that that was taken into consideration.

I see that very considerable sums are to be voted in these -supplementary estimates for the -construction of mew armouries in certain towns in Ontario. I would be glad if the hon. Minister of Militia would give us a statement of the policy of his department in connection with the construction of buildings for our militia in central towns in this province. A considerable number of towns have been recognized but a still larger number seem to have been forgotten.

My hon. friend (Mr. Blain) will understand that it is impossible to do this work all at once. It will involve between one and two million dollars, and perhaps more, to properly house the different militia corps throughout this country. We are going on as rapidly as possible throughout the country, and I assure my hon. friend that we are selecting the places in which these buildings are to be constructed on the advice of military men and from a non-partisan, a purely military point of view. With regard to the rural districts and the smaller towns where there is only say, one unit, my idea is that we should construct a substantial building which can be headquarters, armoury and storehouse, and with a room sufficiently large for a lecture room, where the officers who take an interest in military matters can bring their men together in the evening, and, by means of blackboards and so on, illustrate military affairs and give necessary instruction. This is the idea I have, and that I hope to be able to begin to carry it out in the near future. My plan will include every village of any importance in the Dominion of Canada.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: How many years will it take to carry that out V

I think it can be done in five or six years, and that the total cost will be in the neighbourhood of a million and a quarter or a million and a half dollars.
Mr. COCHRANE What has been done with reference to the armoury in Cobourg ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: The site has been procured, the plans are about complete, and advertisements for tenders will appear at an early day.
I should have added that there is a vote in the estimates of a lump sum for the Public Works Department for the construction of smaller armouries.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: Not the Public Works.

At any rate, the places have not yet been selected, all of them at any rate. If my hon. friend has any particular place in mind, if he will bring it to my attention, I shall be glad to consider it.
M. BLAIN. I brought this matter to the attention of the government at two former sessions of parliament. I may say that the Minister of Militia has been very very kiud in the matter. I would like to know if the town of Brampton, the headquarters for the 36th Peel Battalion, which is a rather important militia corps in Ontario, has been provided for in the general vote ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: I have not the information at hand, but I will make a note of the matter and will be able to give my hon. friend the facts when the Militia estimates are before the committee.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENSE.

speechtext: I may say that the 36th is a very large and rather important corps. At present they have practically no place for the storage of their arms, and the officers are complaining constantly. They find the membership of the company is decreasing because of the difficulties under which the corps labour. I do not wish to complain, but it does seem that some one must be at fault if even a small amount cannot be appropriated for the purpose of remedying this state of affairs. I think the suggestion of the Minister of Militia is a very good and reasonable suggestion, and I hope he will be able to carry it out in the near future, and that some appropriation will be made for the corps I have referred to.

I would point out that the regimental district Joins the city of Toronto and the county of York, and the very fact that he complains of in relation to the regiment, is verified by the condition of affairs there. Many of the officers of that regiment belong to the city of Toronto, and the entire absence of armouries or places where the officers can meet and instruct and drill their men, has a tendency to diminish greatly the number of officers from the county, and the young officers in the city have taken the places of those who belong to the county. I know of no place in the rural districts where an armoury is more needed than in the county of Peel.
I hope the minister will take into consideration the claims of Orillia, where no less than three companies have their headquarters.

I desire to draw the attention of the minister to the fact that there is a cavalry company and an infantry company having their headquarters at Col-borne, and who complain of insufficient accommodation. Colborne is so far away from Cobourg that the cavalry have to have a sto'Fage room of their own.

The minister, I hope, will also provide for the filling up of that)
' skeleton of a skeleton ' of a regiment that is centred in the county of Haldimand.
I think the member for Haldimand (Mr. Thompson) hit the nail on the head when he said that it was simply ridiculous to expect men to go to drill for 50 cents a day.

While provision is being made for drill sheds in various parts of the country, I would call attention to the condition of the drill shed in the town of Flesherton, which is now getting into a bad condition of disrepair from leaky roofs. It was erected by the government a number of years ago, and the officers have repeatedly made application for money to repair the roof and to put the building in fair condition for drill. They have an armoury in the building well fitted up but unserviceable owing to leaky roof. I have heard the officers complaining again and again that they cannot get an appropriation for repairs.
Toronto drill hall-additional accommodation tor new corps, $20,000.
We are obliged to the hon. gentleman for this appropriation. Is it expected that this sum will be sufficient to give the additional accommodation that is required ?

No, I do not think it will. I feel strongly on this question, and I think that we should do something and do it promptly, and in order to make a beginning we are asking for this vote.

speechtext: This heating system has been in operation for 40 years and is working very unsatisfactorily. The air accumulates in the radiators, and the consequence is a terrible noise, which is a great nuisance. This work is intended to be done by the present staff. The chief architect has made up a detailed estimate of the cost, and he thinks this will complete the work. The noise is something fearful, and the clerks are complaining all the time. In addition to that, it does not give the heat it should.

In this connection, I would point out that the ventilation of this House could very easily be changed for the better, the only drawback to a perfect ventilation being the fact that the fans make a little noise. I have examined the apparatus since the subject was up the other evening, and I am satisfied that the system is almost perfect as it is, if it was only put into operation, but it is never operated because the fans make a little noise; therefore, the machinery is shut off, and the consequence is that we sit here breathing foul air. The thermometer at this moment registers over 70. I would suggest that the fans be removed a little higher up, and we can change the air every two minutes.
The attention of the chief architect will be called to the matter.

I may say, at the same time, that I do not think the lighting is as good as it should be. The lighting of this chamber is not at all as good as it was under the former system.

We do not advertise for tenders. There are only three manufacturers in Canada making these things.

At Gananoque, Ottawa and Toronto.
What about the Newmarket one ?

That has its head office at Toronto. When the different departments apply for equipment these firms are asked for figures, and they give us quotations on the specifications and requirements of the different departments.

I understood that there was not a fair distribution of these contracts, that the Ottawa manufacturers were not satisfied with the proportion of the cabinets that they were asked to supply to the government.
What amount of goods of this class was purchased from the Newmarket Company last year, or from the company which has its head office in Toronto ?
I have not that information here. But I will have a statement made out and lay it on the Table of the House, or I will give it to my hon. friend, of the different purchases that have been made.
Is it a fact that the hon. Postmaster General (Hon. Sir William Mu-lock) is a large stockholder in the Newmarket Company ?
I do not know, but I would assume that there would not likely be any foundation in the fact for the statement that the hon. Postmaster General is interested in that company in any way.

I am sorry that the hon. Postmaster General is not here at the present time, 'but it must not be assumed that the hon. minister cannot be interested in that company. In the first place, Newmarket is in the hon. gentleman's constituency. The hon. Minister of Agriculture was interested in a stock company that had very large transactions with this government, in a company that was taking thousands of dollars from a department. It is quite true that the hon. Minister of Agriculture transferred his stock to a near relative. Perhaps the hon. Postmaster General may have followed the good example of the hon. Minister of Agriculture, and transferred his stock to a near relative before having any dealings with the government. Perhaps, when the matter comes up again, the hon. Postmaster General may be here, and we can renew the question.
Yes, let him speak for himself.

I may say that in the town of Newmarket the hon. Postmaster

General is credited with being interested in this company.

I would like to ascertain just what the plan is that has been adopted. There are three firms manufacturing these steel drawers and rollers. It is proposed to take $63,000 for the purpose of purchasing this equipment for the departmental offices. What plan is adopted ? Are public teuders asked for, or are circulars simply sent to these three firms ? Sixty-three thousand dollars is a very large item.

Most of this money is to pay for orders that have been given. Since I have been in the department I have not given orders to any of these firms. I think when there are only three manufacturers if they are all asked for prices, we can get as low a price as if we advertised in the papers. There is quite as good competition as if we spent money advertising in the papers.
Surely the hon. minister does not understand that to be the proper policy in respect of public competition ?

What would my hon. friend do if he wanted to buy cheaply and there were only three manufacturers in the country ? Would my hon. friend spend $40, $50 or $100 for advertising in the papers instead of asking the three manufacturers to submit prices ?

I would. I would have no hesitation, and I think the country would justify the hon. minister in spending $40 or $50 in advertising and asking for tenders for supplies involving an expenditure of $63,000.

Let me inform the hon. gentleman that this is made up of 25, or 30, or 40 items. This is not for $03,000 worth of supplies to be furnished at one time. The various offices apply for small quantities at different times.

I understand that. I think the equipment is about the same in each of the offices. I am not complaining about that. It seems to be modern and up to date. But surely, when the hon. minister asks for $63,000 to be appropriated for a specific purpose, the public would expect that he should ask for public tenders. The hon. minister will not say that he is always posted as to how many firms are in a position to supply these goods. It may be that there are many others than the three manufacturers to whom the hon. minister has referred who are in a position to supply them. It will be quite within the range of possibility that these three manufacturing establishments may hear of this discussion and will understand the policy of the government. We can readily understand that it would be an easy matter for them to come 410
to an arrangement whereby each would supply $20,000 or $25,000 worth, and there would be no competition at all. I think the public will expect the hon. minister to change the policy of the department, if that is his policy at the present time, and that when he is going to ask for supplies to the value of $63,000 he will put an advertisement in the papers and allow all the people that are overdue ? If I understood the supplying this class of goods to tender, so that the public will understand that there is public competition rather than that three manufacturers in this country should simply be asked to submit prices for the supply of these goods.

Are we to understand that the hon. minister during the coming year is going to expend $63,000 on these articles, or is this vote applicable to articles of this class that have already been supplied, and if they have been supplied, to what extent ?

I will have to have a full statement made out In the accountant's branch as to wliat is due and what orders have been previously given. Applications come from the various departments. This would not supply all the applications of various departments for these equipments, but It will cover the most urgent ones and pay the orders that were previously given. I will make inquiry and bring down a memorandum.

For the orders that were given in the past, is the House to understand that no tenders were called for, but that the hon. gentleman's department obtained a certain portion from each one of these three companies, and that the three companies settled the price that they were to uniformly charge ? Is that correct, and if so, is it to be the practice this year ?

It was suggested that the department should ask for quotations from all parties in the business, and where a special article is being manufactured by three or four firms oqly, I think every business man will agree with me that better results are obtained from this system than from advertising in the public press, unless it be that you purchase in the United States. The Auditor General, who is very strict in regard to accounts of this kind, holds that where there are only a few well known reputable firms manufacturing special articles, it is quite sufficient to ask them for tenders by mail. The officers of the department would lie able to judge if tile prices were fair, and they would know if there was any attempt to unduly enhance the prices.
The majority of these post office fittings are imported from the United States, and are not made in Canada.
Since I have been in the department, I have never given an order outside of Canada.
The postmaster In my town supplies them himself, and he biings them in from the United Statets.
It is not done by the department.

But here is a supply costing 165,000, and instead of publicly calling for tenders, you ask three firms to make offers, and leave it to some gentleman in the department to decide whether or not the price is fair. Suppose you carry that principle out further ; if there are three mail routes running out of a village, the Postmaster General will not arrange privately to have the service performed, but will call for tenders, even if the cost is only $50 a year. Here is a contract for $05,000, and no tenders are asked. It is strangely suspicious that the company that is getting the largest end of the order, is a company which I am informed the Postmaster General is supposed to be interested in ; and even if lie is not so interested, they carry on business in the leading town in his riding. -

There is no order given for more than $2,000, unless the department were fitting up a very large building and it would not be more than $5,000 at the outside. I have no particular objection to advertising, but I believe it to be a waste of money.

I am rather suspicious that there is something in it, for the reason that I am bound to say that there are no tenders called for these large red boxes on the street corners in which you put newspapers. They are made up at a little foundry in Aurora, in the riding of the Postmaster General. I know that, because I saw one of them placed on the train the other evening, when I was coming through. The Postmaster General is simply bringing grist to his own mill in every direction. We had an example of it here a few weeks ago, when he was dragging and collecting mail bags from one end of the Dominion to the other. I am still strong in the suspicion that the Postmaster General is one of the stockholders in this company and that lie has been using his influence not to have public competition, but to be able to place the orders for these goods at their own
price.
Mr. BI-AIN. What proportion of this $05,000 has already been expended ?

I will bring down that statement.

BI-AIN. I differ fr m the minister regard to the method of purchasing goods. I admit, that if tenders are for, they should specify that the

goods should be manufactured in Canada, but I do not think that the minister or his department should be the judges as to how many firms in Canada are in a position to supply these goods. Whether that be right or wrong in the interests of the government, it is certainly not in the interests of the people. The practice advocated by the minister in this respect will at least be always open to suspicion. I think the minister should state to the House now, that in future, he will ask for public tenders and give every man in the country an opportunity to supply these goods. How does the minister know that there are only three manufacturers of these articles in Canada V I think I could put my finger on half a dozen manufacturers in Ontario alone, who would be able to turn out these goods. It may be said that these three are the largest firms, but if it is understood that the government will put this contract of $65,000 a year up to competition, and give it to the lowest tenderer, there is no doubt in the world but that others will engage in the business.

As this was a special line I got my information from the chief architect, and the deputy minister that there were no other firms in this business in Canada ; but after the assertion of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Blain),
I certainly shall try an advertisement, and see whether we get any returns from it or not. I have no desire to favour one as against another.
Hear, hear.

The minister said he thought the public interest would be protected, because the officers of the 'department would be able to judge by the prices asked, as to whether there was any attempt on the part of the manufacturers of these articles to unduly increase the price. What experience have the officers of the department had in the matter of the manufacture and procurement of articles of this class ? How do they know that there is not a combination, or whether the prices are proper prices ?
They can make the comparison only from their experience and by getting prices from other countries where these goods are manufactured, and comparing them.

Will the minister also bring down copies of any circulars or pricelists the officers have obtained from foreign countries respecting the Rvalue of these goods? I would also like to have information as to the quantity of these goods purchased, the names of the firms who Have supplied them, and the prices in each case.

I will bring this return down. My hon. friend asked how the officers could make these comparisons. I did not say they had

made them, still the chief architect tells me that he is sometimes called upon by representatives of foreign firms, and he may have some of their price lists. If he has any price-lists or circulars from foreign firms, I will have them brought down.

It is a fair business proposition that if these goods are manufactured in Canada, Canadian manufacturers should have the preference, but it is not a sound business proposition to say : There are only three firms manufacturing these - goods in Canada, and we will not advertise for tenders, but will send a circular to these firms, and buy from the firm putting in the lowest tender. I would ask what proportion of the vote asked is to pay accounts that are overdue ? If I understood the minister, he has not himself contracted for any of this work, but is asking for this money in order to pay accounts outstanding.
The MINISTER OF rUBLIC WORKS. I will bring down the information.

How much of this vote is intended to be expended for this purpose ? The sum of $63,000 should furnish a very considerable amount of space. It is not intended to provide fire-proof accommodation, I presume. I have seen these steel drawers in the safes of municipal and other large corporations where there are a great many documents to preserve, and I should think some system of that kind would be much better. With $63,000 worth of drawers you should accommodate a great many documents, and I will ask how much my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works expects to expend in that way ?
The MINISTER OF rUBLIC WORKS. The instructions to the officers are that after paying the accounts that are due and settling for the orders given, the expenditure is to be kept within the amount voted. The amount would be divided amongst the partments according to the judgment of the officers as to which is the most urgent. The system referred to by my hon. friend is a good one, but it would be very expensive. This is intended more for files; the shelves are equipped with rollers for handling heavy books. With steel instead of wood fittings they are much more satisfactory, and are, to a great extent, fire-proof. The accumulation of dust, &e., on the wooden shelves makes them very inflammable.
Will the minister also bring down a statement of the full amount that has been expended for these modern office furnishings during the five or six years since their introduction.

I have promised to bring down tin first memorandum immediately, because it is cue that I can have made in an hour or so. The second one I will also bring down, but it will require a little more time.

I suppose there must be some fire-proof accommodation in some of these buildings for certain documents.

I do not think there is any fire-proof accommodation in Ottawa outside the vaults in the Department of Finance. The intention is to ask parliament at an early date for a vote for the construction of a fire-proof building, not necessarily a large one, in which the records and archives of the country may be kept without danger of destruction by fire.
I thought that in the repairs to the west block after the fire, the building was made fire-proof.

The building is supposed to be fire-proof.
Kingston-Royal Military College drill hall,
This vote is included at the request of the Militia and Defence Department for the erection of a hall at the military college to be used as a drill hall and skating rink combined.
For the amusement of the cadets ?
Both for their amusement and their instruction.

I notice the absence of any item providing for the furnishing of a water supply for the college. The present water supply is very inadequate. As the Minister of Militia and Defence knows, a number of the students were attacked with typhoid owing to the fact that they were using water polluted by the drainage of the city of Kingston. The engineer of the Militia Department is proposing to employ a suction system of water supply. He proposes to have a station near the college buildings, to extend the in-take pipe out in the water, and to draw the water to the college by suction. For all the difference in the cost, it would pay the government to place the pumping station over on Garden island, to have the in-take pipe in the pure water beyond the island, and to force it across to the city. The only extra cost would be an additional half mile of pipe, and as the pressure on the pipes would be from within, no pollution could enter them through any leak that might occur in the pipes under the bay, whereas the suction under the system proposed by the engineer would draw any impurities into the pipes.

I am very glad the hon. gentleman has brought this matter up, and I will call the attention of m.v officers to it. I had understood, however, that the water

which it is proposed to bring in had been tested, and had been found satisfactory. I may say also in this connection that I think that there was some slight doubt as to whether the fever was due to the water supply or to the milk supply, or some other cause. At any rate, it was found that the milk supply was not what it should be. To remove any possible doubt, we decided to change the water supply, and while there is no item for the purpose here, there is_ an estimate in the main estimates providing for this change. The engineers and scientific people connected with the college, as well as the officers of the department, have looked into this matter, but since my hon. friend (Mr. Hughes') has referred to it-and I know he was on the spot not very long ago as one of the visitors of the college-I shall call the attention of my deputy to it.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext:
The United States have recently voted $5,500,000 for additional improvements at West Point and they propose voting during the coming vear another $8,000,000 for the same purpose. Now for an institution like the Royal Military College, where the finest young engineer officers are being prepared for civil and military life in Canada, I would recommend the minister not to do any cheeseparing in providing this water supply. If he places the pump-house, as I may call it, on Garden island and has the in-take pipe on the other side of the islaud where he can get absolutely pure water, he can force it across the bay. Then, whether the pipes leak or not the water will go through pure, because the pressure will be outward. The systnn proposed by his engineers is to put a pipe out into the bay on which the military college stands, and have the in-take beyond what is called the danger limit. Then, with the pump house on the main shore, the water will be drawn in. Experience shows that these pipes are never water-tight. The movement of the waves, a touch by an occasional vessel, tlie dragging of an anchor, *will cause leakages, and then, with the suction, the foul water will be drawn into the pipe. I trust the hon. minister will bring this matter before his engineer. And ht him not be content with the report of his own officer. The engineer is not specially informed about these matters. If he will not take into consideration the elements of a proper water supply let the hon. minister consult any sanitary engineer. I am sure that such a man will not endorse for a minute the proposition of the engineer of the department, but will insist on having the other method ; and I am sure that the House and the country will support the minister in any additional expenditure that may be necessary.
