From this it is evident that the reason given for setting aside Mr. Coleman's tender must fall to the ground. I make bold to say that before that reason should have been accepted by the head of the department, he should have seen that closer inquiry was made as to the real cause of the delay in the construction of that exhibition building. He should have made inquiries from the architects and builders of the city of Toronto as to Mr. Coleman's standing. I think that under the circumstances a very grave injustice has been done to Mr. Coleman. I have a lot of information respecting Mr. Coleman's status, and it is of the most satisfactory character. Mr. Coleman stauds the peer of any other contractor in the city of Toronto in his line of carpentering. I will read another letter :
Hamilton, Ont., April 17, 1903. To whom it may concern :-
This it to certify that we, the undersigned, have been doing business with A. B. Coleman, general contractor, lately of the village of Burlington, during the past ten years or more. He bas carried out a large number of contracts from out of our office, and carried them out well and faithfully and fully up to the requirements of the plans and specifications and to the terms of his contracts, and to our entire satisfaction in every case. We have always found him to be a pleasant and an honest man to deal with, never found him trying to shirk any of his responsibilities with us, and we would without any hesitation upon our part give him any contracts from our office that he tendered upon, provided he was the lowest tenderer. -
We highly recommend him to any party or parties who may be Intending to build any
structure. We may further say that during these many years of business with him we have never been under the unpleasant necessity of speaking an unkind or unpleasant word to him on account of any of his contracts from our office.
This document Is signed by W. H. Stewart, architect, Hamilton, formerly of Stewart and Strickland, architects, Toronto. I have also a communication from Richard A. Waite, architect of Buffalo, N. Y. The Minister of Public Works knows the imputation and standing of Mr. Richard A. Waite as an architect. He stands very high in that profession, is one of the foremost architects in the United States, and has carried through to completion some of the finest buildings in Canada, amongst others the parliament buildings in the city of Toronto. This is what Mr. Waite saye :
To whom it may be of interest :
Within the past few years, Mr. A. B. Coleman has fully carried out several contracts both large and small under my supervision, and in the matter of time as well as competency and responsibility, highly commendable.
This is dated from his office in Buffalo on the 22nd of April, 1903. I have another one from Mr. C. J. Gibson, known, X presume, to the minister as another one of our leading architects. This is dated from bis office in Toronto on the 23rd of April, 1903.
To whom it may concern :
This is to say that Mr. A. B. Coleman, general contractor, has within the past ten years put up a great many buildings for me, some of them very large and important, and he has always carried out his contracts quickly and intelligently to my entire satisfaction, and I can confidently recommend him as competent to complete any contracts he undertakes expeditiously and conscientiously.
I will read one more communication in connection with this matter, as I do not wish to take up the time of the committee-I will read a letter from the city clerk of Toronto, Mr. W. A. Littlejohn, dated 27th of May, 1903 :
My dear Mr. Clarke,-I have your favour of the 26th instant, asking whether Mr. Coleman, the contractor for the carpenter work on the main building in the exhibition grounds, has been reported as being derelict in his work or not. Mr. Geo. W. Gouinlock is the architect for the building, and in reply to an inquiry told me over the telephone to-day that he had a line from you and would write you to-night giving the fullest information possible on the subject. I may say that there has been no formal complaint laid against Mr. Coleman. There has undoubtedly been delay in the completion of the building, but other trades seem to be responsible.
I do not think, Mr. Chairman, that I could make out a much stronger case than I have made. I present these documents to the committee and I enter an emphatic protest against the action of the department. Here is a case where public tenders are asked for and where responsible contractors reply to the advertisements calling for tenders, and

put in their bids on work the department contemplates, giving their marked cheque as security for completion of the work. I say I emphatically protest against the course that has been pursued in this case, a course that must be inimical to the public interest, in ignoring the lowest tenderer and giving the contract to another one who is probably $400 or $500 higher. I make no complaint at all against Mr. Carlyle, for 1 am fully convinced that Mr. Carlyle has had a good deal of experience, but in fair competition his bid was some $500 higher than that of Mr. Coleman. I repeat it is most unfair and unjustifiable under these circumstances, in view of Mr. Coleman's experience and reputation, to have put his tender aside and given the contract to another contractor.

I would be very sorry if any injustice has been done to the gentleman who tendered. When my hon. friend brought the matter to my attention I furnished him with a copy of the report and other evidence of what the architect actually did. I had no knowledge whatever of Mr. Coleman myself. At that particular time it was notorious that the city architect asked a committee of the council, I think, who had this work in charge, for Mr. Coleman's dismissal from the work. There was considerable difficulty between them.
The hon. gentleman is thinking of another work entirely different from this one.
Who was the engineer in charge 7
Mr. Gouinlock.

It would have been a great mistake on the part of the architect, for the sake of a few hundred dollars, not to have brought this matter to the attention of the department. There was no feeling in the matter, and any action that was taken was based upon these reports. I am sure the chief architect had no feeling at all against Mr. Coleman, and he was guided in his action by tbe conviction that Mr. Coleman was not able to carry on the work. My hon. friend perhaps has forgotten the reports that appeared in the papers at the time, of the discussion over the difference that existed between the architects in charge of that work and the contractors.
There was no architect that I know of.
My hon. friend will remember that I handed' him a report at the time, showing there was great difference between the architect himself and the contractor.

There was a difference of opinion between the architect and some of
Mr. CLARKE
the contractors for other portions of the work that were required to be put into this building. Theye was no difference, so far as I remember, between the architect and Mr. Coleman. The fact that the architect has given me the letter that I read is the strongest proof that I am right in my contention. I have read for the information of the minister the statement from the city clerk of Toronto, I have also read the opinions of leading architects, men who are in the front rank of the profession, to show that the reasons urged, at least one of them, that this man was dilatory in his work, was not well founded. It may be merely a coin-, cidenee. There were three tenders presented for the work. Of course politics would not enter into consideration in 'awarding the contract. There were three tenders submitted in response to the request of the department. Mr. Coleman's was the lowest. The next was Mr. Carlyle's and the next was from Messrs. Brown & Love. Mr. Coleman's was set aside, Mr. Carlyle was given the contract for the post office at his own figures and Messrs. Brown & Love were given a contract to repair, alter and block up the custom-house without any tenders at all. It may have been only a coincidence, but still it does not look very well, to say the least of it. It is a matter, I respectfully submit to the hon. minister, that ought not to be permitted to occur again in his department, if there are going to be bona fide public tenders for public work. If people are invited to tender, if they give the security and they have a reputation for doing good work, their tender being the lowest, they ought to get the contract.

Whether it is a coincidence or not, I can only say that I have given the committee the reasons that influenced the architect in coming to the conclusion that he did arrive at. It may be, as my hon. friend says, that it was not the fault of the contractor that delay was caused at the exhibition building, but that it was due to delay on the part of some other contractor. It certainly appeared by the newspapers as if it were the fault of the contractor.
Mr. Gouinlock, the architect, pointed out that the delay was entirely due to the contractors for the structural iron and the steel work.

I would be very sorry if it should appear from the evidence that he was a very capable man and that there was no reason why he should not have carried out the work satisfactorily, but it was only on account of the difficulties that were found to exist, and that were reported in the press, between this contractor and the architect that this action was taken in regard to the work on the post office.

Mi'. CLARKE. The secretary of the exhibition board, in a statement regarding the matter, says that the work was :
In no way delayed by any lack ot ability on the part ot Mr. Coleman. I believe him to be thoroughly honest and in earnest and in this case working against very great difficulties.
One of the difficulties being the failure of the Canada Foundry Company to complete their contract for the structural iron work. While having the greatest possible respect for the permanent officials of the department, I hardly think that sufficient investigation was made by these gentlemen. I think if they had gone to Mr. Gouinlock, who was the architect under whom Mr. Coleman was doing this work for the Exhibition Association, or if they had gone to the secretary and manager of the Exhibition Association, who was vitally interested in having the work done as speedily as possible, or if they had gone to the city clerk of Toronto, who is responsible for the accuracy of the minutes of council and the care and filing of any documents which are presented to council, he might have obtained reliable information. I think the chief architect was not justified in making the report that he did against Mr. Coleman, which gives Mr. Coleman such a black eye, and which resulted in having his tender set aside, without having gone to the officials who are directly responsible and who are interested in the matter. He should have applied for a statement of the facts to the secretary of the Exhibition Association, Dr. Orr, or to Mr. Littlejohn, the city clerk of Toronto. Before Mr. Coleman was turned down either one of these officials should have been consulted about it. I have presented the facts, and I will leave it to the lion.' minister to say whether he thinks Mr. Coleman was fairly dealt with.
This letter admits that there were difficulties, but the only question is as to whether there were such difficulties as Mr. Coleman could control.
Tour architect might have found out if he had gone to the proper person and inquired.
The city architect did not seem to know that, because he had taken the unusual step of taking the work out of the contractor's hands. It was on that action that this recommendation was made.

I did not quite gather what the reason was for not accepting the lowest tender, because it seems to me there is something more in this than has yet appeared. There is a question as to why the lowest tender should not be accepted. Was the reason given in the report of the chief architect ?

I will read the report which the minister sent to me :
Public Works. Canada,
Chief Architect's Office,
Ottawa. November 6, 1902. Sir,-Referring to the tenders for the additions and alterations to the Toronto post office.
Tenders were invited for the works referred to, by public advertisement, and three tenders were received as follows :-A. B. Coleman, $21,470; David Carlyle, $21,949, and Brown & Love, $22,238.	.	.
The principal work to be done consists in taking down the present vault, removing the greater part of the basement and the first floor rear main walls of the building, putting in foundations and the provision of iron columns and girders to carry the upper stories of the rear main wail.
As this class of work is both difficult and dangerous, proper precautions will have to be taken, otherwise serious results to the building might follow.
There being only a difference of $479 between the two lowest tenders, as above shown, I would strongly recommend the acceptance of Mr. D. Carlyle's tender. Mr. Carlyle has done considerable work for this department in the past and he has been found an efficient and reliable contractor. Further, as the work will have to be done so as to interfere as little as possible with the post office officials and the public, and part of it will, in all probability, have to be done at night ; any delay or dispute that might arise with the contractor would be a very serious matter. .
I have been informed that Mr. A. B. Coleman is the contractor for the Industrial Exhibition building at Toronto fair grounds, and that the said building was to have been completed for the fair held in August last, but at that date it was not ready for the roof owing to misunderstandings and disputes with the contractor.
The foregoing are my reasons for recommending the acceptance of Mr. Carlyle's tender.
I have the honour to be. Sir,
Your obedient servant,
(Sgd.) D. EWART,
Chief Architect.
Fred. Gelinas, Esq.,
Secretary, Department of Public Works.
The only reason given was the alleged delay on the part of Mr. Coleman in completing the work at the exhibition building.

There were these two reasons :	First, at
the time it was urgent that this work should go on. It was important when dealing with a large building and removing some of the stone and iron pillai-s, that the work should be placed in the hands of an experienced contractor. Secondly, it was a matter of public notoriety that Mr. Coleman was at serious variance with the architect in charge of the work at the exhibition grounds. I am sure my hon. friend would say that under these circumstances we would not be warranted, even if be were a good contractor, if he had more work than he could do, in giving him this contract. The explanation which the hon. gentleman has given to some extent puts a different face on the matter, but this serious difficulty seemed to exist between the

architect and the contractor. These two reasons, that is the reason of urgency and the difficulty which I have mentioned, no doubt influenced the chief architect in recommending the acceptance of Mr. Carlyle's tender.

I would be inclined to think that the matter had been dealt with in a very casual way, in so far as inquiry into Mr. Coleman's ability is concerned. There are two reasons assigned for the course which was adopted. One is that the highest tender was from a contractor who had already done considerable work for the department and had been proved an efficient and reliable contractor.
That is no reason as against Mr. Coleman. That is no reason why he should not have got the contract.	.

I quite agree. I quote the language of the gentleman who makes this report.
I have been informed that Mr. A. B. Coleman is the contractor for the Industrial Exhibition building at the Toronto fair grounds, and that the said building was to be completed for the fair held in August last, but at that date it was not ready for the root owing to misunderstandings and disputes with the contractor.
That deals with the matter in a very casual way indeed. He does not tell us from whom the information came, but he simply says, that he has been informed of so and so. The fact that Mr. Coleman was contractor for a building that was not ready at the time agreed on, is no basis for a charge against Mr. Coleman, unless he were in default in some way.. There might be a dozen reasons why the building was not completed in time, none of which would in the slightest militate against the acceptance of Mr. Coleman's tender in this case.
I do not think the minister was justified in accepting so indefinite a charge against Mr. Coleman as a reason for putting aside the lowest tender. It would be the duty of Mr. Ewart or any one else, before making a report on which the lowest tender was rejected, to inform himself explicitely as to the facts. If loose methods of this kind are to be followed, you could set aside almost any tender. You could get such a report against almost any contractor who ever did any work in Canada. We discussed in the House last year a case where a contractor had hardly commenced some work in Manitoba at the time the contract should have been completed, and I do not think anyone would venture to say that that gentleman is not an efficient, and able, and capable contractor. There is only one reason given in the letter, and it is a mere hearsay reason and after all it does not charge anything. It says, that the building was not ready for the roof owing to misunderstandings and disputes with the contractor, but It does not necessarily follow that the con- | Hon. Mr. SUTHERLAND.
tractor was not perfectly right in every position he took with regard to that matter ; it does not follow that the people with whom he was dealing were in the right and yet on a casual, indefinite, inconclusive statement of that kind, this man's tender has been set aside, and the next highest tender has been accepted. I do not know anything about Mr. Coleman ; I never met the gentleman; I never heard of him before to-night, bnt I do say that in the public interest, it is not right that the tender of Mr. Coleman or of any one else should be set aside by the minister, or by any of his officers, by reason of any such inconclusive and casual statement as is contained in this report.

I will admit that the delay in carrying out the work would not of itself be a sufficient reason, but there was evidence attached to that memorandum which I think will change the opinion of that gentleman very much. They wanted this work done immediately and if my hou. friend himself knew that a man had more work than he could do, he would not likely employ him to do work which had to be done in a hurry. There was a statement originally appended to that report which showed that the architect had publicly asked the committee for the discharge of that contractor.
I suppose the minister will produce the document containing that statement ?
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Clarke) must have forgotten that it was pinned to tiiat report when I handed it to him.
I haqded the hon. minister back the documents which he gave me, and I was afterwards sent a copy of the letter which has been read.

It was reported in the newspapers that the architect in charge of that work was asking the committee for the dismissal of the contractor on account of these delays and disputes and misunderstandings, and for other reasons. I will give my hon. friend a copy of the document which was attached to that, and I think he will see that our action was perfectly warranted. I would be sorry indeed if any injustice had been done to Mr. Coleman.

I am dealing with the case presented in that report, which does not refer to any other evidence being attached to it. I can hardly understand how the architect, Mr. Gouinlock, could have been calling for the dismissal of Mr. Coleman in view of this letter which is produced by my hon. friend (Mr. Clarke) :
Toronto, June 8, 1903.
Dear Sir.-Replying to your favour, I would state that Mr. A. B. Coleman, contractor for the

carpenter and joiner work on the manufacturers' building, industrial exhibition grounds, is not responsible for the delay caused in connection with the erection of this building. The delay in this work is almost entirely due to the contractors for the structural iron and steel work. Mr. Coleman's contract on this building is about $18,000 and he has given the work every attention and carried it out in a manner satisfactory to myself.
Was that the architect who had charge of the work ?
He says so.
I suppose I have a copy in the department of the report, showing the proceedings before the committee, and if I have I will bring it down, and the hon. gentleman can judge for himself.

The rest of this letter of Mr. Gouinlock, refers to other work which Mr. Coleman is said to have performed in a satisfactory manner under the superintendence of Mr. Gouinlock. If Mr. Gouiulock's statement can be relied upon, it is absolute proof that Mr. Coleman was not responsible for the delay charged against him.
If the statement as reported in the papers is correct, it would put a different phase on the question.

I do not wish to take up more time now, but I present this view of the case to the minister : Mr. Coleman is a well known contractor in the city of Toronto. If reports appeared in the newspapers condemning the work done by Mr. Coleman, and if the officer of the department thought these reports were sufficiently important to justify him in making the report he did, it was only fair to Mr. Coleman that the officer of the department upon whose recommendation he was turned down should have gone, first to the architect who had charge of the building for the city and the Industrial Exhibition Association, or second, to the city clerk, or third, to the secretary and manager of the Industrial Exhibition Association. The architect of the department, so far as I know, ignored these gentlemen, who were in a better position than any one else to give him reliable information. Suppose the most inflamatory statements against Mr. Coleman had appeared in the newspapers. Even that would not have justified the architect of the department in making a report derogatory to Mr. Coleman without being advised by the gentlemen most intimately connected with the work that those reports were accurate. If the hon. gentleman will bring down the information he has, we shall learn what allegations were made against Mr. Coleman by the architect of the exhibition building ; because I shall be surprised to learn that Mr. Gouinlock asked permission to dismiss Mr. Coleman, and afterwards wrote the letter to me which I have read. Under whose supervision, may I ask, is this work being done ?
Mr. Curry, I believe, is the local architect.
Had the department any communication from Mr. Curry advising that Mr. Coleman's tender be not accepted ? Was it upon his advice that Mr. Coleman was turned down ?
No, there was no communication from Mr. Curry.

The more this thing is investigated, the less creditable it appears. Mr. Curry was the local architect, the gentleman who looked after the construction work on government buildings in the city of Toronto for years before this contract was given to Mr. Carlyle. As a matter of fact, Mr. Curry was an alderman of the city of Toronto at the time, and I believe is yet. Was it not extraordinary that the chief architect of the Public Works Department would pass over Mr. Curry, the local architect, and take a newspaper report as his reason for asking the minister to turn down Mr. Coleman ? He did not consult Mr. Curry, a local architect of standing, under whom the work was being done, nor the secretary of the Industrial Association, nor the city clerk. Might I ask the minister, when bringing down this information, to ask the chief architect why he did not think it worth while to obtain information from Mr. Curry ?
St. Catharines drill hall (revote, $10,000), $20,000.

A vote was taken for this work some time ago, but a dispute arose as to the site which had been chosen being unsatisfactory ; and after some delay, the city secured another site which met with'the approval of the Department of Militia and Defence and the Department of Public Works. The contract amounts to $56,000, and the work is now going on.
Is the city furnishing the site ?
Yes, a fine site.
What will be the total cost ?
The total cost is estimated at $85,846.
How many regiments does it accommodate ?

I think there is only one regiment at St. Catharines.
Sault Ste. Marie-public building (revote, $10,000), $25,000.
What is the cost of this to be ?
It js estimated by the architect to cost $S8,-395. Tenders are now being advertised for.
Has a site been secured ?

Yes. 'It was procured in January, 1902. It cost the department $8,200, and the locality contributes something. There are 84 by 100 feet at the corner of Queen and East streets ; also lots five and six on East street, 56 by 81 feet.
For what reason are you erecting a public building of this kind at Sault Ste. Marie ?

There is no proper accommodation there. My hon. friend knows that the place has grown very fast and that there are some very large manufacturing institutions there. Last year the postal revenues amounted to $18,551 and the customs duties to nearly half a million dollars.
What purpose is the building intended to serve in addition to a post office ?
The Customs and Inland Revenue Departments.

In what part of the town
is the site, and from whom was it purchased ?
It is in the old part of the town. It was purchased from Mr. J. Dawson and Mr. W. H. Plummer. The marine office will also be in this building.
Is that building of stone ?
Stone and brick.
Is the time for receiving tenders yet up ?
No ; the tenders are due some time this month.

$S5,000 seems an extraordinary expenditure for a town the size of Sault Ste. Marie, when towns of the importance of Owen Sound and Peterborough and others throughout Ontario have no public buildings, and others of equal importance have buildings costing from $15,000 to $20,000.

I might say that three weeks ago a friend of mine called on me and I asked him how things were getting on at the Soo. He said that the worst fea-' ture was that they could not get their mail matter delivered. A number of families had to club together so that the ladies of these families would get the letters in turn during the day time, because when night came the post office was so crowded that they could not begin to get the mail. Such a condition of things as that should be remedied.
Woodstock-public building. $5,500.	-
This work is under contract.
I understand that this is in the constituency of the hon. minister. What is the necessity- for erecting this building ?

The necessity is that Woodstock is the most important town in Ontario. The revenue is also larger than that of any other town.
I suppose that the government some years ago thought that it was proper to have a public building there. It is a very modest building, and this is to pay the balance on the contract.
I would not have mentioned this matter if the hon. minister had been as generous with his gifts to others. The only thing I regret is that he did not consider North Grey.

I think that Owen Sound must rank next in importance to Woodstock.
Brantford drill hall-additions and alterations, $15,000.
What is the size of the addition being made to this hall ?

One hundred and seventy-five feet by one|

hundred feet. The city allows us to extend the building twenty feet on the side of the park. This provides a hand-room, shooting gallery and other improvements.
Is it the intention of the department to level the armoury grounds at St. Thomas ?
Neither the chief architect nor myself has any recollection of that matter being brought to our attention.
The armoury would toe almost useless if the grounds are not levelled.

I will bring this matter to the attention of the lion. Minister of Militia and Defence and see what report he has received. We deal with matters of this kind in connection with the Department of Militia. Representations are made to them by the local officers.
I am simply drawing the attention of the minister to the necessity of this work.

They appear to have taken it off our hands as satisfactory ; the St. Thomas building was completed some time ago.
St. Mary's-public building, $8,000.
This is a new work, which it is estimated will cost between $20,000 and $25,000.
St. Mary's is in Perth and so is Stratford. Stratford has already a large public building. The minister had better give up that rule as an excuse.
Has a site been purchased for the St. Mary's building ?
No.

The population of St. Mary's is 3,400 and the total revenue derived by the postal authorities is $0,000.
I would ask the hon. minister what justification there is for this building, and what it will cost ?
The total estimate, including the site, is between $20,000 and $25,000. This is not for a post office alone, but for all the departments of the public service.
Has a site yet been selected '!
No.

Would the minister explain why he is spending $25,000 in St. Mary's-not that I at all object to St. Mary's having this public building. St. Mary's has a revenue of only $6,000 and a population of only 3,400. Why does he give
it a public building at a cost of $25,000, when he refuses a public building to Owen Sound, with nearly 10,000 inhabitants and a revenue of about $15,0C0 ? The minister lays down a principle as justifying the building a post office in one place, and yet refuses to recognize that principle in other cases. There is something very unsatisfactory about the way the money is distributed for public buildings.
I have already said that if the hon. gentleman thinks I have left Owen Sound out of consideration he is mistaken. I do not leave unconsidered the case of Owen Sound.
How much will the site cost V
I have no figures on that subject. The amount I have quoted includes the cost of the site.

I do not think it will do Owen Sound a great deal of good to have my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Sutherland) merely consider it ? He considers Owen Sound, but when it comes to the other places he gives them appropriations. We have had instances of town yielding not one-fifteenth of the revenue yielded by Owen Sound and to which the publie buildings are given. We had one in which the revenue was $612 and another in which the revenue was $838. As my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Sutherland) has got beyond the consideration stage with regard to these towns, why is it he cannot do the same with regard to Owen Sound ?

It is all the more to be noted because, as I said this afternoon, the town of Owen Sound, which is really a Conservative town, has, since 1890, given Liberal majorities because lion, gentlemen opposite have been promising them a public building and public works. Even in the late election, Owen Sound gave a Liberal majority of 33. They gave the late representative, Dr. Horsey, a Liberal majoiity. And when the Minister of Customs ran, they gave him a majority of over 100, because he promised them something in the way of a public building and public works. But now, when they see some of the smaller towns, such as St. Mary's and Woodstock, and other places, having large sums of money spent on them, while Owen Sound, the most important town in Western Ontario, receives not a single dollar, they begin to wonder what the promises of hon. gentlemen opposite are worth.
Oshawa-public building, $8,000.
This is a new work. What is the building to cost when completed V

Between $20,000 and $25,000. The post revenue is $7,000, and the customs duties

nearly $28,000. Oshawa is a very prosperous town.
Is there a public building in Whitby, in the same county 7
I do not think so.
Whitby is the county town, a very important town, and larger than Oshawa.
I am afraid my hon. friend is not always precise in his information. I think he will find that Whitby is not so large as Oshawa.
It is the county town and an older place than Oshawa, and a very important town.
It is a very important town and a very pretty town, and some day

I understood some time ago that we were going to have a new system, and that when a public building is proposed to be built we should have a proper estimate of its cost, instead of carrying on the old system of having a certain sum voted and then coming down year after year for more money to complete the work.
I hope the Minister of Public Works will inaugurate the new system and stick to it.

In every one of these items I have given the committee the maximum estimated cost, and I have stated that if, on completing the plans and getting tenders, the price greatly exceeded the estimate, I should not feel justified in going on until I had further consulted parliament.
What will the electors of South Ontario think of their representative, who lives in Port Perry, not securing a public building for Whitby, the county town 7

I think I am quite capable of looking after the interests of South Ontario. 1 am very pleased to be able to say that Oshawa should have a public building. We in South Ontario are very proud of Whitby and Oshawa, particularly proud of Oshawa as an industrial centre. The hon. minister gave the returns for Oshawa for 1902. I have the returns for the year ending the 30th of June, 1903, and they show that both the post office and customs revenues are increasing rapidly. While, for 1902 the post office revenue was about $7,100, for 1903 it was over $7,900-or nearly $8,000. And, while the revenue from customs for 1902 was $28,000, last year it amounted to about $35,000, showing a splendid growth. The town has an electric railway and its industries are going ahead very rapidly. They have an old shack of a post office there, in fact the post office is kept in a store. The Hon. Mr. SUTHERLAND.
accommodation is not at all suitable for the town, and I have been able to convice the minister that Oshawa deserves this public building. While Whitby is the county town and while we are very proud of it, while, as the hon. member for North Grey (Mr. Thomson) says it is an old and important town, and in my opinion it should also have a public building, still, Oshawa seems to need this building at the present time. I think this vote will meet with the approval of the people of South Ontario.
Has there been any correspondence between the municipality and the government with regard to the site ?
No.
What proportion of this money will be paid for the site 7

I do not think I am in a position to give the hon. gentleman (Mr. Blain) any direct information. It is a growing town, but I should think a -site would not cost more than $4,000, or $5,000 at the outside.
Perhaps the hon. member for South Ontario who is familiar with the locality would be able to give us that information. No doubt he has been consulted.
He wants to boom prices; we want to keep them down.

The hon. member for Peel (Mr. Blain) asked me a question about the site. There is nothing definitely settled that I am aware of regarding the site. I think it would not be wise to say where the site is to be, because perhaps the price of the property might advance. But I am advised that the prices of property have been rapidly advancing in Oshawa during the past year or two. A good many buildings are going up, but no doubt the government will be able to get a site suitable for the purpose.

How many sites ha^ the hon. gentleman in view ?
Toronto-additional postal station, $25,000.

Where is this branch post office to be constructed 7
The MINISTER OF1 PUBLIC WORKS. This appropriation is made on the request of the Post Office Department, carrying out their policy of spreading out these branch stations. This will be station D, I think it is on Yonge street.
Deserouto public building-to pay balance due on contract. &c., $1,500.

What does that building cost altogether.
The MINISTER OF PUBLIC W'ORKS.
It is estimated that $25,000 will cover every-

thing, including the site, furnishings and so forth.
I notice on page 7 of the supplementary estimates, sessional paper No. 5, there is an item of $4,500 for a Deseronto public building. Does one item include the other, or are they separate ?

That was for the year 1901-2, and was to pay a contract then entered into. This is to complete the whole work.
Brilgeburg-public building, $5,000.
This is to build a custom-house at the end of the International bridge. The building is estimated to cost $10,000.
What is the population ?

Less than 2,000. But it is not built on account of local business, but at the request of the custom-house authorities there. Officers are stationed day and night at the end of thql bridge, where a good deal of travel takes place between the United States and Canada.
Hamilton public building-alterations and improvements for inland revenue purposes, $5,000.
Are these improvements to be made on the new property that has been recently acquired ?

Yes.
Windsor public building-repairs, improvements. &c., $1,300.
This is practically for new letter-boxes.
Are they put in by tender ?

All by tender.
Picton public building-to complete, $1,000.
Could the minister say what work has been done on this building, if any ?
It was for levelling, sodding and a sidewalk. The retaining wall is to be paid out of this. This will complete the whole work.
The laying of this sidewalk is a very small affair, and the levelling and sodding amount to next to nothing. The whole job could not cost $200, but I see the appropriation is $1,000.
The sidewalk, including the excavation and the levelling, cost $4G0.
There was no excavation, only a little sand had fallen in, that is all. Was this part of the original contract ?
No, this was not done by contract, it was done by some of the local authorities, at so much per foot.
How much per foot was paid for it ?
The chief architect thinks it was eighteen cents a foot.
Is not that an extraordinary price ? There is hardly a town in Canada pays more than ten or twelve cents a foot for a concrete sidewalk.
My hon. friend had better look at the city of Ottawa and see what they are paying. I think he will find that they are paying over eighteen cents.
Was there any tender for this work 1
No, not exactly. Prices were asked for. As this is only to pay a balance due, I have not got the detailed information, but I can get it for the hon. gentleman.
This cannot possibly be the balance due on the work the minister mentions. I would not consider the whole work was worth more than $200.
I will give my hon. friend a memorandum, and he can see what it is.

I think this is a justification for the argument which was set up here a while ago, that asking for prices from contractors is not quite satisfactory. There is nothing like public tender. Asking for prices leaves an opening for extortionate charges, and I am sure the hon. minister must admit that 18 cents a foot for this work is entirely too much. It is 50 per cent higher than iis paid in almost any town in Canada, and it must be very unsatisfactory to the people of Picton, who are having this work done. They are charged $400 odd for work which might have been done for two-thirds of the amount.

I agree with my hon. friend that up west they have been getting these sidewalks built for an average of from 12 to 14 cents a foot, but down here it seems to be more expensive. I was rather surprised to notice a few days ago that in the city of Ottawa they are paying 18 cents a foot. However, I will get my hon. friend the information he asks.
I am quite sure the town has not paid nearly that price for a large amount of similar walks laid down durifig the past couple of years.

Then I must be mistaken, because I am

sure the chief architect would not, unless some misrepresentation was made, pass an account which exceeded the municipal price.
Ottawa departmental buildings-new elevator for west block, $6,000.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Who is putting that in ?

This will be let by contract.
Toronto drill hall and armouries-contribution towards paving Armoury street with brick and laying a concrete sidewalk on University street, $2,645.

We intend to make a contract for these improvements.
Toronto military buildings-magazine, $3,000.
These magazines are being erected at the request of the Militia Department.
Is this to be constructed on the old ordinance reserve land at the west end ?

I would not like to speak with certainty, but I think so.
London military buildings-magazine, $3,000.
Is that to be built on Carling Heights ?
I expect it will be built on Carling Heights.
Will this $3,000 finish the work ?

These sums are put in at the request of the Militia Department, which says that $3,000 will be the cost of these magazines.
Ottawa public buildings-new coal shed, $10,-
000.

I understand that as a result of the improvements which are going on, the property which has been used for this purpose has been confiscated. It will lie necessary to build a coal shed somewhere on the canal basin for our supply of coal. It will be built ou our own land.
Will it be built of cut stone ?
The chief architect thinks we ought to build it of stone. Perhaps it would last longer, but I do not think it will be cut stone.

Would it not be better to put this building up in cement blocks ? It will be much cheaper than stone, and it will be quite as substantial. If 5*ou had a sample building in Ottawa, it would be an advertisement for what is becoming a very important industry in this country. They are manufacturing cement in Ottawa, and it would be well for the
government to put up a building of cement blocks.

I am very much in favour of cement work. It is getting to be a very important local industry, and I shall certainly have the chief architect ask for a report in regard to the price of cement. If it is as satisfactory and cheaper thau stone, I would be very glad to adopt it.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
Why is it necessary to have a coal shed at all ?	1 thought the
government purchased all the coal supplies by tender ?
But we must have some place to store the coal. We use between 6,000 and 8,000 tons, and we must store it somewhere.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Why do you not require the contractor to deliver it as needed, and to store it until delivered ?

We would pay a great deal more for it. It is brought in by water, stored in our own sheds without any cost either to the contractor or to ourselves, and delivered by the contractor from time to time as wanted.

Would it not be rather unwise for the hon. minister to advocate the use of any particular cement stone until it lias been thoroughly tested in this country ? I do not think we have had enough practical experience of it to warrant its being used even upon coal sheds.

I am sorry my hon. friend (Mr. Lefurgey) lives so far back in the country that he i-s not aware of the value of cement for building purposes. In our part of the country we have been using it for years, and we find it very satisfactory.
We have two cement buildings on the Toronto exhibition grounds, and I would invite the hon. minister, if he has not seen these buildings, and if he can spare the time, to go out and see them.
I was through them, and I was very much impressed with them.

They are using cement for curbing and other purposes that it was not thought possible to use it for a few years ago. rrhere is a splendid proposition across the river in Hull, where the finest quality of cement will be turned out. I think the House will strongly support the hon. minister in putting up a building with this cement. It will be an abject lesson, and it will give a satisfactory opportunity of testing it.
There is better cement at Owen Sound.

You can put up the public building at Owen Sound in cement. I certain-

ly think that there should be some public building erected of cement, because this country is going to develop a great business in the production of cement, and if the government will put up one building in cement, it would be an object lessou.

I am quite serious in regard to this matter.
1 will ask for a special report from the chief architect's department.

For the information of my hon. friend from Prince Edward Island (Mr. Lefurgey), I would say that Owen Sound is the original home of the cement industry in Canada, and that some of the finest residences that we have in Owen Sound are built of cement blocks. They are in appearance handsomer than stone, and certainly they are substantial. They stand our climate excellently, and are very durable. I hope the hon. minister, when he is in Owen Sound, will take a look at some of these buildings, and I can assure him that there is nothing in stone that can compare with them.	[DOT]
Do I understand the minister to say that the department purchases a large quantity of coal and stores it away ?

You have to buy coal in Ottawa when it can be carried by water. We receive it in the coal shed, and then the contractor delivers is as it is wanted by the different buildings. It would cost a good deal more unless we had some place where we could store a large quantity.
Ottawa post office and customs-house-improvements, $16,000.
Is this work to be done by tender ?
This work has all been done under the supervision of the officers of the department, and by the men in the employ of the department.
Do I understand the minister to say that the work has been done ?

The work has not been done. The estimated cost of this work is a little over $15,000. composed of a number of small items, it is done under the supervision of our own officers.
Kingston Royal Military College-stable, $5,000.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Will this be let by tender?

Yes. I questioned the estimate of the Militia Department, but they told me they could get the kind of stable they wanted for this sum.
Sarnia-public building (revote), $1S,800.
What is the explanation of this 1
It has already been voted, but the work was not completed in time to pay it before the end of the fiscal year.
Was it let by tender ?

Yes. The contract was $62,000, and this money is to pay the contractor.
Toronto examining warehouse-addition to, $25,000.
What kind of an addition will be erected ?
This is to build an addition to the warehouse 70 feet by 44, and four stories high. The estimate of the chief architect is $30,000.

Of course, the work will be let by tender ?
Cobourg-improvements, $5,000.
What Is this money for ?

This is for changes and improvements in the Cobourg post office. The hon. gentleman knows that this is a building which did not receive any attention for a long time, and it had fallen into a bad state of repair. This will cover the total cost of the work.
Is it to be done by contract ?

Yes.
Kingston-barracks for Royal Canadian Field Artillery, $25,000.

This makes provision for the construction of new barracks at Kingston, with the understanding that the money will not be spent until after the sale of the present barracks which are reported to be unfit for occupation, owing to the impossibility of affording proper drainage. The TSte du Pont barracks are to be disposed of for the benefit of the crown.
Is the minister going to dispose of the site of the T5te du Pont barracks ?
I am taking this vote on that condition.
Where are the new barracks to be located ?

I think the city offers a new site, and speaking from memory, it is on the present fair grounds, which is said to be very suitable. I estimate that the present property will bring us $40,000 or $50,000, so that the whole change can be made at a cost of some $40,000 or $50,000 to the country. However, I will ask the Minister of Militia to

give further information when his estimates are under consideration.
What is the total cost of the building to be ?
Do you mean the total cost to the country ?
That is what we are interested in.
I understand it will be $40,000 or $50,000. The total cost of the work would be three times that, including the site and so on.

Fifty thousand dollars would not commence to erect a barracks with the necessary buildings, and so on. It is a reflection on Canada that new barracks have not been provided in Kingston years ago. The present barracks have no sanitary arrangements ; they are old buildings some of them dating from the time of Frontenac. The minister should be very careful about these plans, and he should have them examined critically by more than one authority before adopting them. Does the hon. gentleman intend to restore old Fort Henry, so as to make it habitable, or at least presentable ?
I have no appropriation for that purpose at present.
This building is costing between $45,000 and $50,000 ?

No, it is costing between $100,000 and $150,000. I am taking this vote on the condition that the arrangement is carried out. I said that the city would present a valuable site, the old exhibition grounds, and the present barracks are to be sold, and, I understand that the difference between the value of that and the total cost will be $45,000 or $50,000. We are doing this, as hon. gentlemen know, at the request of the Militia and Defence Department.
Hawkesbury-public building, $5,000.

This is quite a prosperous place. The last census gives its population as over 4,000. We have not been able to lease or rent any accommodation for the post office, and the people have sent in a large petition for a building. We propose to erect one costing $6,000 or $8,000. The place is a large manufacturing place and the revenue is very considerable.
What about the site.

The site will be very cheap.
Ottawa public buildings-paving front of parliament building, tar macadam, $6,900.

This, is an item in which all the members Hon. Mr. SUTHERLAND.
of the House are very much interested. I think the matter has been brought up in the House at different times, and strong representations have been made as to the disagreeableness of the dust. We think that may be overcome by having the ground paved with asphalt or tar macadam. We have taken a vote for the cheaper pavement, tar macadam.
Wingham-public building, $8,000.
Give us some information about this building. Wingham is a very important town doing a good business.
I will take the minister's place, if any information is necessary in regard to the Wingham building.
speakername: @Deputy Chair(man)? of Committees of the Whole

speechtext: The population of Wingham is 2,392, the postal revenue $4,507 and the customs revenue $6,449.
In what riding i$ Wingham ?
In the riding of the chairman of the committee.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I would just say to the members of the committee that Wingham is one of the best commercial centres west of the city of Toronto.
- Chiefly Tory isn't it ?	.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I will come to that. It is one of the best commercial distributing centres. It is served by two branches of the Grand Trunk Railway and one branch of the Canadian Pacific Railway. We have no less than six passenger trains leaving and six arriving each day, in addition io freight trains. It is also a large manufacturing centre. It has a large foundry and stove factory. It has several woodworking factories, furnishing material for house building. It is also one of the largest furniture manufacturing centres in the Dominion of Canada, employing in that industry between 300 and 400 hands. There are four furniture factories, though they are now combined under the furniture syndicate of Ontario. We have also v*ry fine buildings, including three banks. It is one of the prettiest towns that any of you ever saw. Our streets are veritable avenues, lined -with beautiful maple trees. We have no less than fourteen miles of granolithic sidewolks, for which we paid $25,000.
How many hotels in the town ?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am not so much interested in the hotels as I am in the general welfare of the town.
To whom does the hon. gentleman assign that work in his campaign ?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I get very little support from the hotels on the Tory side. If I were asking for this on political grounds, it would he different; but the town has only one public building. Unfortunately for themselves and the welfare of the country, a majority of the people of Wing-ham vote against me ; but nevertheless, I am not going to forget them in the days of their necessity, and I am asking for a post office, not for any political or personal purpose but because the town needs a public building.
Has the Deputy Speaker purchased a site yet ?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I will come to the site. I have been serving my party here for the last seventeen years, and I may say that if this grant is given it will be the first public money that has ever gone into East Huron since the' first tree began to grow there.
You had the rake-off in some other way.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Therefore I do not ask it for political reasons ; I ask it because we need it. The present post office is situated in an inconvenient locality, and it is not adapted for post office purposes. Eor the year 1901-2 the postal revenues amounted to $4,500 ; for the year ending the 30th of June, 1903, we collected $4,806. In addition to that the customs collections for 19012 were $6,500 and for 1902-3, $9,303 ; and so far this year they amount to $1,000 a month. When a town of that size and character demands a post office, I do not think there is a single man on the opposition benches who will say nay. I leave it in their hands. With regard to the site, we have several available. I do not think the site is going to be very dear, though I would not like to mention any sum. There is a site in view which I think will be selected if the owner is willing to sell it at a reasonable price. If not, the council will probably look elsewhere. I may say that this vote is only an instalment. To put up a building that would be in keeping with the other buildings that will surround it, would involve an expenditure of from $16,000 to $20,000. The bank of Hamilton stands on one corner, a magnificent structure, and the Dominion bank has fitted up a building across the street from it in a style that is equalled by very few banks in the city of Toronto. It is a brick building, which the bank has rented for twenty-five years. These bank buildings are covered with slate. On the other corners there are splendid buildings, and we want the government to erect a building that will be in keeping with them. We take a pride in keeping our town as clean and neat as possible. and if any of you visit it, vou will 411
come away with the impression that it is one of the prettiest and neatest towns west of the city of Toronto.

We have listened with some interest to the very eloquent address of the Deputy Speaker regarding the town of Wingham. I may say that we have in the constituency of Grey three towns that can claim everything that has been said on behalf of the town of Wing-ham, and in some cases a good deal more. Something has already been said about the town of Owen Sound. I doubt if there is in the whole of Canada a town of its population, with such important manufacturing industries and with such a great commerce, that has not had one dollar of public money expended in it for public buildings. Then I come south to the town of Durham. I asked last year for a public building there. It is a thriving and prosperous town, with a population of double that of some towns that are getting handsome buildings. And a little further west of Durham we have the town of Hanover which has no less than four furniture factories and other-manufactories as well, j-et it has never had a dollar of public money expended in it for public buildings or for any other purpose. While lake ports claim a good deal for their harbours, or docks, or elevators, or dredging, inland towns like Durham and Hanover have no claims of that kind, and therefore no public money is expended in them. I would again ask that they should have some fair consideration. In some cases too much money is expended on large ornamental and expensive buildings for post office and custom-house purposes to the detriment of other smaller places. The hon. member for North Grey (Mr. Thomson) has already spoken for Owen Sound. I doubt if there is any town of its size in the whole of Canada which has been so neglected as it has been in regard to public buildings.
What is this building in Wingham to cost ?
Between $20,000 and $25,000.
The minister will remember that he is breaking the rule he has laid down. There is already a public building in that constituency at Goderich.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Goderich is thirty-five miles away.
The minister should admit the principle that their votes are all based on political expediency and necessity.

I find that the members of the government are being provided with public buildings in their own constituencies. The Minister of Customs has a building at Brantford, the Minister of Public Works at Woodstock and the Deputy Speaker at Wingham. I do not know how they have come to side-track the Postmaster



General. I would again point out the inconsistency of erecting a public building in a place of 2,200 inhabitants, with a revenue of about $4,000 or $5,000, while no public building is erected in the county town of Grey, with a population of 10,000 and a revenue of $10,000.

I would ask the hon. minister if he has received any application for a public building from the town of Listowel ? Listowel is not very far from Wingham, and is one of the most important towns in that part of the country. If Wingham and other towns are to get favours of this kind, Listowel should have some assistance in the way of a public building ; a post office and custom-house are badly needed. It is a large shipping and manufacturing centre, and 1 would like to see something done for Listowel.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
I think it is a wilful waste of public money to spend such a large sum as $20,000 or $25,000 in building a post office in a small town containing 2,000 or 2,500 population, which has no prospect of becoming a very large town. This is an inland town, and a post office costing $10,000 would be quite sufficient. When the Conservative government was in power I asked for a public building in my town, which is a large manufacturing town, and a post office was built costing $10,000 or $12,000 at the outside. The town gave the site and the government put up a building at that price. To spend $20,000 or $25,000 in a little village like Wingham is a wilful waste of public money. The government should establish a rule that unless there is a population of a certain number and a revenue of a certain amount the town has no claim at all. In the case of a frontier city like Toronto or Montreal we should, in the interests of the country, make our buildings respectable buildings, but to meet all the requirements of a post office building, which is all that is needed at Wingham, a building costing $8,000 or $10,000 would give all the accommodation required.
Mr. I-IUGHES (Victoria). Listowel has a revenue of $4,496.77 and Wingham a revenue of $4,507-a difference in the revenue of about nine dollars.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I have a statement from the Post Office Department showing the statistics for Wingham for this ' year. It is as follows :

And during the last three months, $1,000 per month.

I might say that Listowel is a magnificent town, equal-Mr. THOMSON (Grey).
ly entitled to a post office, and I would be glad if the minister could see his way clear to gratify the request of my hon. friend from North Perth (Mr. MacLaren).

I had the pleasure of visiting Listowel the other day in company with the hon. member for North Perth (Mr. MacLaren), and I was delighted with my visit. It is a right smart town, the very centre of the great cheese industry. Experts in the cheese business come from the old country to visit its great cheese market very frequently. It is growing steadily, it has many fine business establishments, a great many beautiful private residences, and is in fact a thoroughly modern up-to-date town. Everything that has been saidifor Wingham can also be said for Listowel. If there should be a public building in Wingham, Listowel should stand a good chance also. It is a great manufacturing centre in a fine agricultural district, with large cheese, butter and other products. I strongly support the proposition of the hon. member for North Perth (Mr. MacLaren) that something should be done in this case.

I agree with the representations made as to the importance of Listowel. It is near my own home and I know it well. We are proud of Listowel. I had not thought particularly before of the matter to which my hon. friend from North Grey (Mr. Thomson) drew my attention, but I think he will find there is not very much party politics in this list of public buildings. If he will run his eye over the list, I think he will find that very little favour has been shown to the Liberal constituencies to the neglect of the others. ,

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: You are bribing the others.

No, I think the applications have been considered very fairly. Going over the list, I think any impartial man would be surprised to see how many strong Conservative towns represented in this House by Conservatives are receiving post offices or other public works. I shall be glad when I have an opportunity, to remember the requirements of Listowel.
Every new public work in this list is for a riding represented by a Liberal in this House.
Who is the Liberal member representing Stratford V

There is no new public building there.
The MINISTER OF PUBLIC W'ORKS. Yes.
An armoury. I was speaking of the list of post offices.

I am going to make a strong appeal on behalf of Meaford

which has been added to the constituency of North Grey. Here is a splendid town, situated in my constituency as at present constituted which, I think, should have a special claim. It has a population of 1,916, and a postal revenue of $3,199, while the amount paid in post office orders is $26,000. It is one of the most important towns on Georgian bay and is the centre of a splendid agricultural district. Its inhabitants are a fine, industrious class. The town has a splendid harbour and I am glad to say, the government have done something to improve it of late years. I would make a special appeal to the Minister of Public Works for a building for Meaford.

I think we are dealing very liberally with the harbour of Meaford and my hon. friend (Mr. Thomson, Grey) must give some of the inland people a chance. I know Meaford is a fine growing town, and after some of the inland towns have been provided for, I hope we shall be able to meet the requirements of Meaford.
Stratford-armoury, $10,000.
What is to be the cost of this building V

About tiie same as the others.
Woodstock-armoury, $10,000.
What is to be the total cost of this building ?
About $25,000-the same as the others, Stratford, Sherbrooke, &c.
Has the site been purchased ?
No, I think the county council will contribute to the site. They have communicated their intention of doing so. There is a first-class regiment there of eight companies.
In Woodstock, or in the county ?
In and around Woodstock.

I would point out to the minister wbat was incidentally touched on before, that in centres like Stratford, and Woodstock too the militia is growing. In a short time Stratford will have a city battalion of its own, and, likely a battery of its own. Woodstock should have cavalry, being in the centre of a fine agricultural country where many people own horses. I think the minister would do well in preparing the plans, to provide, as far as possible, for housing the artillery, and for storing the saddlery in case cavalry units should be formed.
411+
Do I understand tlie county council will furnish the site in Woodstock. If this is so, who furnishes it in Stratford ?

What I said was that we had had a communication from Woodstock asking with regard to the plans, showing the local interest in the militia there. The county council, irrespective of politics, are anxious to contribute something, as they do from time to time, in the payment of the militia.
Public works-chargeable to income-Manitoba-Winnipeg-district military stores building, $10,000.	'
Where is this building to be erected ? At Fort Osborne ?

This is to provide for the erection of a building for military stores, district No. 10, Winnipeg, to contain (A) the mobilization stores for troops of the province of Manitoba, and (B) quarters for the foreman of stores and district offices This is to be constructed at tlie request or the Department of Militia and Defence.
Winnipeg-new immigration building and postal station, $60,000.

This is to provide a new immigration building for the reception of immigrants in the city of Winnipeg. It will contain also Dominion land offices and accommodation for the Post Office Department for sorting mails, i&c. The intention is to erect this building near the Canadian Pacific Railway station. This is represented by the Department of the Interior to be a matter of most urgent necessity. They are suffering now for want of accommodation in this respect.
Is this building intended to take the place entirely of the present immigration hall ? Is the present immigration hall to be dispensed with ? If so, this amount is entirely inadequate.
I may say to my hon. friend that we are adopting a scheme submitted by the imperial authorities. The total cost of this building is $125,000.
The present immigration hall is about 60 feet by 250 feet in length, three stories high. This $60,000 will not build a building one-half that size.
By what department has the plan of this building been prepared ?
By the Department of the Interior.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext:
The present building, as any one knows who has visited Winnipeg and seen it, is unfit for the purpose to which it is assigned. The com-

partments in which the immigrants have to sleep are placed around the sides of the wall, and are much like stables. In these narrow compartments the immigrants and their children have to sleep and dress. There is no ventilation, and very little light. I trust that in the plans that are being prepared, some attention will be paid to these requirements. The present immigration hall is situated on a low flat spot, which is very muddy in wet weather. Some attention should be paid to the sanitary condition of the buildings.
/ Mr. McCREARY. The building the hon. member speaks of is merely for the temporary detention of immigrants on their way through. They remain over night and pass on the next morning. This new building should not be so close to the station, but should be one or two blocks removed.

What the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. Hughes) says is quite correct, that every provision should be made in the form of bath rooms, closets and that sort of thing, for the sanitary welfare of the immigrants.
Is it the intention to retain the old buildings and to make a separation between the immigrants, some of them being of an inferior class ?

I understood that in the plans submitted it was the intention to retain only the hospital building.
Winnipeg-addition to public building, $40,000.

If there is any place in Canada which requires increased accommodation frequently it is the post office at Winnipeg. The chief architect has reported plans for building two additional stories, a new stairway and an elevator, in the Winnipeg public building, at a probable cost of 865,000.
Will you be able to start on this work at once ?

The plans are being prepared, and as soon as this vote is given, instructions will be given to proceed at once.
Winnipeg military buildings-quarters for noncommissioned officers including guard-room, &c., $6,000.
Winnipeg military buildings-^magazine, $3,000.
Does the Minister of Militia and Defence know where this magazine is to be situated in Winnipeg ?

I cannot give the exact point, it is near the city of Winnipeg. I may say with regard to these three votes at Winnipeg that that city is becoming an important depot, a point at which military stores Mr. HUGHES (Victoria).
must be placed. At present we have no suitable buildings there for that purpose, and it is absolutely necessary, as the country is filling up, and if we are to pretend to defend it, or to assist the civil power, that we must be in a position to do so. These buildings are being constructed for the purpose of bolding military stores which will be sent west. As to the magazine, I cannot give the exact location, but it is at or near the city of Winnipeg. The previous item of $6,000 is for the accommodation of noncommissioned officers who are now living, some of them in rented houses ; and as we have plenty of ground, it is thought much better to build our own houses for these men.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: As this is a military item I want to ask the Minister of Militia a question relating to the item of $25,000 for the barracks of the Royal Canadian Field Artillery at Kingston. I want to ask if there is in that appropriation an amount included for repairing the martello towers around the harbour at Kingston? They were dismantled by storms two or three years ago, and have been allowed to fall into disrepair. At Fort Henry also the walls are tumbling down, and everything is becoming dilapidated. I think in the interest of the country these martello towers should be kept in a first-class state of repair. I drew the attention of the department to it last year, and fully expected that provision would be made this year for taking proper care of that property.

There is a vote for general repairs out of which a sum might be taken for the purpose the bon. gentleman mentions. I quite agree thatthese repairs should be made, unfortunately, we have not bad money to do it with. With respect to this vote of $25,000 at Kingston, I would like to explain to the committee that the city of Kingston has offered the government a block of land, some twenty-five acres, used now for exhibition purposes. The city offers that as a free gift to the government in the -event of our wishing to construct new barracks. The present barracks are found to be unsanitary, and productive of fever. There appears to be some difficulty in disposing of the sewage of the city in such a wTay that it will not be a nuisance to these barracks. It is intended to sell the property there and realize what money we may, and to construct a new barracks probably on this land, although I may say that at this moment the question is being considered of restoring the Fort Henry property. I know that the deputy minister who has been there and has examined the property thinks that we might occupy that with great advantage. I spoke to General Lord Dundonald the other day about it, and he is very much inclined to that view, ' so that it is possible that this vote may1

not be used. I think it is only fair to the committee to make this statement as to what is going on.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I fully agree with the view of the hon. minister, because the government have any quantity of land east of Fort Henry, and it will be a better site than that in the city.
I think so, too.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: If you want a healthy location, you have it at Fort Henry and upon the ground east of it, along the river front.
In regard to this group of items, will these buildings be erected by tender ?

Yes, except the repairs to the immigration building.
North-west Territories-Edmonton jail-(revote, $5,000), $35,000.

This is under contract.
Prince Albert court-house and post office, $10,000.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Is that the total amount ?
This is being erected on the recommendation of the Department of Justice, and it is a necessity there.

As soon as the territories get provincial autonomy the new provinces will erect their own court-houses. A post office is certainly necessary there, but I think the court-house part of it might be reconsidered, as it is a provincial more than a Dominion building. It is quite evident that the hon. minister does not intend to give the territories provincial autonomy.

I do not say that. So long as the territories are under the jurisdiction of the Dominion, and as the country is filling up very fast, we must of necessity meet their requirements. I have not the total cost of this building.
It looks as if it was going to be one building-a courthouse and a post office.
Yes.
If a province is created there this building will have to be handed over to the province as a courthouse, or else retained and used for some other purpose.
Even if it is, at an early day more space' will be required at that place.

Certainly.
Moose Jaw-public building, $5,000.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: What is this building for ?

A post office. We will have to make some provision here, as there is a rapidly increasing population at Aloose Jaw. I understand that the post office receipts increased by over a thousand dollars last season and they will have increased this season probably by a very considerable amount.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: How expensive a building are you going to put up ?
This building will cost between $15,000 and $20,000 ; but in view of the rapidly growing population, I will have to ask the House to give me sufficient latitude to enable me to reconsider the matter.
Has Aloose Jaw no public building at all ?
No. The customs receipts increased by $2,000 between 1901 and 1902. When I get a full report from the officers, I propose to recommend the erection of a building suitable to that growing place.

This is the headquarters of the Pasqua branch of the Canadian Pacific Railway, although it really branches off at the junction a few miles down. I think this is a very small building for a town like Aloose Jaw.

I will take that into consideration.
Barracks for permanent corps (Strathcona Horse), $10,000.
Where is that to be located ?
I am not prepared to say. The Alilitia Department made representations that it is desirable to erect a barracks at some place hi the North-west Territories.
Is it to be in Edmonton or in Strathcona 7
Some representations were made that Calgary would be a good point, but no decision has been come to in regard to that. It depends on the representations made by the military authorities.

Is there going * to be an increase in the permanent force ?
The AIINISTER OF A1ILITIA AND DEFENCE. Yes, by about 100 men.

Are you going to retain the police force in the same region ?
The AIINISTER OF AIILITIA AND DEi FENCE. The police force is gradu-

ally being moved to the northward, and as it is moved forward the militia will take its place in the southern portions of the territories. The police will vacate the barracks at Calgary. It is intended to establish a new militia depot at Calgary, and the police will be moved northward from Calgary to Edmonton. The police will transfer, I expect, their accommodation at Calgary to the new military depot, and it is probable that this accommodation will be quite sufficient.
Oh, no ; not for a hundred men.

Well, for eighty men. It is sufficient at any rate for a good start. Perhaps it would not be inopportune to say now that the depot which is to he established in the west will perpetuate the name and fame of the Strathcona Horse. All the contingents which served in South Africa have their names preserved in different branches of the permanent force, except that of Lord Strathcona. It was thought fitting that the memory of this one should be perpetuated, and it is proposed to call this one the Strathcona Horse.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

When I was there last fall, the building was about to be occupied and appeared to be completed.
This is to pay the contractor for fittings for electric light, &c.

What was the total cost.
' The MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS. $76,666.
The Minister of Public Works stated last year that the work was under contract for $49,000, and now we are told that it has cost over $76,000.

That was the contract price for the building, but the cost of the site, fittings, furni-Sir F. W. BORDEN.
ture, letter boxes, heating, electric light, &c. had to be added to that.
Vancouver-public building, $60,000.
What will the total cost of this be ?

It will probably cost in round figures $100,000. The city is growing very fast and' accommodation to about that extent is required. We are now paying very heavy rentals and I think it is a good business proposition to have all our offices in one building in Vancouver.

Last year we had a statement that a certain building would cost $49.000, but we now find that it has cost over $80,000. Is the minister giving us the same kind of an estimate with regard to this building ?

I must be fair to the late Minister of Public Works, and state, that in that case he gave the contract {mice. If he were asked about the site and so cm he would have given the information. I have stated on several occasions to-day, and I repeat that my desire is to state to parliament the maximum estimated cost in each case. I have said that if after we advertised for tenders it was found that the cost would be considerably more than I stated, I would not go ou with the work before coming back to parliament.
What does the minister mean by saying that the Vancouver building will cost $100,000.

Plans have not been prepared for that building, but I consider that a building suitable to the requirements of a growing city like Vancouver will cost about $100,000. If it shall be found to cost very much more than that, I would feel that I should come back to parliament.
Does the Minister mean that $100,000 will include everything ?

Oh, no. I understood the hon. gentleman to ask the cost of the building. The total cost including the site and everything will be more than that. I will not ask parliament for another vote-for this until I give full information.

That is where the misleading part of it comes in. The minister should give us a plain matter of fact statement as to what the total cost to the country will be. Every one knows that a building in this country has to be heated and equipped. If that equipment costs about as much as the building itself, the public are misled.

In almost every case, I have endeavoured to give a fair estimate of the total expenditure. This is the first instance to-day in

which we have not sufficient information to give that estimate, and I say that if it exceeds greatly the amount I have stated, I will not go on with the building until I inform parliament what the estimate is. In almost every case I mentioned to-day, I have included the total cost.
Rossland armoury, $10,000.
These buildings in British Columbia will cost about $10,000 if built in wood, and $15,000 if built in brick. The Rossland building is expected to cost not more than $15,000.
How many companies are in the town of Rossland ?
I think only two.
With regard to these public buildings in British Columbia, will tenders be advertised for, and will the work be given to the lowest tenderer ?

That has been done in the case of all the works under construction. The two new works will be let by tender and contract.
